notes.reason: The sentence is Parnas's own summary: "Nineteen states also passed 88 new worker-protection laws in 2025, including paid leave in Virginia and a near-total ban on non-compete agreements in Washington." He is not quoting or disputing anyone. I checked both sources word for word: the Virginia governor's release is dated May 11, 2026 and opens "Governor Abigail Spanberger today signed landmark legislation creating a paid family and medical leave program", and the Littler alert opens "On March 23, 2026, Washington Governor Bob Ferguson signed Engrossed Substitute House Bill 1155". The underlying report is the State Futures and NYU Wagner Labor Initiative brief titled "Workers' Rights Wins from 2026 State Legislative Sessions", whose introduction says the gains came "in 2026", so the whole count belongs to 2026, not only the two examples. The year is wrong in a way that matters: 2025 was the year Governor Youngkin vetoed both Virginia paid leave bills, so the post credits a year that blocked them. The slip is not Parnas's alone. His paragraph tracks the Guardian's September 7 article, which wrote "In 2025, 19 US states passed 88 laws" and named the same two examples, so he copied the Guardian's error, which makes a narrow date correction with official sources easy for him to accept. Nathan may add, as context, that the brief itself covers the 2026 sessions.

notes.reason: Same sentence, same author, and the correction is right. The Washington half is verified: the Akin Gump alert (read through the Wayback Machine, the live page refuses fetches) says ESHB 1155 "was signed into law on March 23, 2026", and the accepted quote is verbatim, including Akin Gump's own slip of calling it "SB 1155"; the note itself correctly says HB 1155. The Virginia half is also verified: the May 20, 2026 release says "Governor Abigail Spanberger today signed landmark legislation to create a statewide paid sick leave program". The veto clause is true but unsourced: Youngkin vetoed the paid family and medical leave bill HB 2531 and the paid sick leave bill in March 2025. Opus worried that the post's "paid leave in Virginia" means the family and medical leave law rather than the sick leave law the note cites. That is not disqualifying: the Guardian sentence Parnas was summarising says "paid sick leave and medical leave passed in Virginia", so his phrase covers both, and both were signed in 2026. What keeps this at uncertain is that it is the weaker duplicate of note 33118868, which names the law the author most likely meant and sources every date, so sending both would be redundant and sending this one alone gives the author an opening to say the note picked the wrong law.
